boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's Lübeck entry (engagement, 6 November 1806) in cohort v1's fourth-coalition 1806 group: the French 1st and 4th corps and the Grand Duke of Berg's cavalry against General Blücher's corps at Lübeck, from the French approach that morning, with the baggage convoy and the Swedish detachment taken on the march, through the storm of the gates to the pursuit that evening and night: Major Ende's capitulation behind Krempelsdorf, Major Witzleben's detachment near Moisling and the surprise of Schwartau, whose prisoners, most of the regiment Kunheim by Höpfner, are placed in this entry's reported losses and not added to Bodart's figures. The Swedes were not Prussian troops, and the claims keep them apart where the sources do. The capitulation of Ratkau on 7 November is B376b; the 29th Bulletin's 16,000 prisoners cover both days and are not split. Travemünde's surrender and General Pelet's capitulation, both later, are outside this entry. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A (French) as 30,000 men under Marshals Bernadotte and Soult and side B (Prussian) as 15,000 men under Lieutenant General von Blücher. By his stated rule his strengths are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. Höpfner gives side B's garrison in battalions and guns, and the 1st corps journal about 20,000 Prussians (claims side-b-strength, side-b-strength-french); no other count of side A was read (claim side-a-strength). 'M.' is Mann and 'Gen.-Lt.' General-Leutnant in Bodart's list of abbreviations. English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the heading and entry: '1806 6/11. engagement at Lübeck (4.)'; 'victory of the French (30,000 men) under Marshals Bernadotte and Soult over the Prussians (15,000 men) under Lieutenant General von Blücher'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian) in Höpfner: the garrison of Lübeck consisted of 13 battalions, to which the regiment Jung-Larisch, 1 fusilier battalion and 6 companies of Jäger were later added, and of 52 guns. At Gadebusch, before the march to Lübeck, the army had lost perhaps 4—5000 men on the retreat through fights, desertion and exhaustion; it still had numerous cavalry, but with very worn horses, and about 100 guns, and only the 1st corps had enough ammunition. After the town was lost, General Blücher had left of the whole garrison only 1 battalion of Oels, 2 weak battalions of Manstein, 2 battalions of Kunheim, 1 battalion and 1 company of Jung-Larisch, the remains of the 2nd battalion Natzmer and the small remains of the Jäger and fusiliers.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images of pp. 272, 283-284 and 292; the 4—5000 was checked on a full-resolution crop (the OCR reads 45000). The passages read give no headcount for the garrison or for the cavalry outside the town. The corps was brought from the retreat, so the claim is tagged inherited. The army's state is cited with the sentence after it, which names General Blücher. English renderings (ours): 'after such arrangements Lübeck seemed in a quite respectable state of defence'; 'the garrison consisted of 13 battalions, to which later the regiment Jung-Larisch, 1 fusilier battalion and 6 companies of Jäger were added, and of 52 guns'; 'the army had lost perhaps 4—5000 men on the retreat through fights, desertion and men worn out; it still had, it is true, numerous cavalry, but with very exhausted horses, counted about 100 guns, but only the 1st corps had sufficient ammunition'; 'General Blücher was therefore also not of the opinion that he should fight at Gadebusch with the greatly superior enemy, but believed that he must first reach a position in which the troops could be granted some rest in safety'; 'General Blücher lost with Lübeck a great part of his artillery, 22 guns without the regimental cannon, and the main strength of the infantry'; 'of the whole garrison there remained to him only: 1 battalion of Oels, 2 weak battalions of Manstein, 2 battalions of Kunheim, 1 battalion and 1 company of Jung-Larisch, the remains of the 2nd battalion Natzmer and the slight remains of the Jäger and fusiliers'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian), side A's (French) figures: the 1st corps journal, quoted in Foucart's footnote to Bernadotte's letter of 7 November, gives the Prussians about 20,000 men on the rampart and around the town with a formidable artillery, 25 pieces on the Burgthor front alone (7 on the isolated bastion, the rest on the curtain, the right-hand bastion and in the tambour), and a corps of about 5,000 men that had come out of the town and taken position under the batteries in front of the tambour. Bernadotte wrote that he drove before him about 5,000 men who had come forward; that the convoy taken after Selmsdorf was escorted by about 1,000 infantry and 2 squadrons of hussars; and that 3,000 men who had come out of Lübeck to cover its entry withdrew in great disorder. At Schönberg at 4 in the morning of the 6th he had written to the Grand Duke of Berg that the enemy had very few men at Lübeck. The Grand Duke wrote that General Blücher commanded all the remains of the Prussian army gathered together.
claims.rationale: Side A's letters and the journal in Foucart's footnote, read from the page images; the 25 was checked on a full-resolution crop (the OCR reads 26). Interested estimates made at different moments, not reconciled with each other, with Bodart's 15,000 (claim bodart-strength) or with Höpfner's units (claim side-b-strength). The footnote closes with its attribution to the 1st corps journal. English renderings (ours): 'Marshal Bernadotte to the major general. Lübeck, 7 November 1806'; 'the Prussians had about 20,000 men both on the rampart and around the town, with a formidable artillery; on the Burgthor front alone they had posted 25 pieces, 7 on the isolated bastion and the rest on the curtain, on the right-hand bastion and in the tambour'; 'a corps of about 5,000 men had come out of the town and taken position under the protection of the batteries in front of the tambour'; 'the ground between the two is entirely marshy, though passable in some places. (Journal of the 1st corps.)'; 'meanwhile I advanced on the town with all the rest of my army corps and drove before me about 5,000 men who had come forward'; 'arrived at Selmsdorf, I and my escort were charged by the enemy hussars'; 'I had 1 battalion of Drouet's division advance, preceded by some voltigeurs, and soon we had in our power a convoy of 300 baggage wagons escorted by about 1,000 infantry and 2 squadrons of hussars, who all laid down their arms'; '3,000 men who had come out of Lübeck to protect the entry of this convoy withdrew in great disorder'; 'Marshal Bernadotte to the Grand Duke of Berg. Schönberg, 6 November 1806, 4 o'clock in the morning'; 'all the reports that have reached me and the result of the reconnaissances I sent out give me the certainty that the enemy has not made the hook towards Wismar that we suspected, and that he has very few men at Lübeck'; 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor. Lübeck, 6 November 1806, 9 o'clock in the evening'; 'General Blücher, who commands all the remains of the Prussian army gathered together, had awaited Your Majesty's troops in Lübeck'.

claims.value: Side A (French): Bodart gives 30,000 men under Bernadotte and Soult; no other count of side A was read. The units named: Bernadotte's 1st corps, with Drouet's division at the head of the attack, Rivaud's division, Dupont's division in reserve behind the town watching the banks of the Trave, and 3 light cavalry regiments under Tilly (the 5th chasseurs and the 2nd and 4th hussars); General Rouyer, with part of his brigade, was charged with the ships carrying Swedish troops at Schlutup, and Höpfner has Bernadotte leave 'General Rougere' there with a half-brigade. Höpfner has Bernadotte follow the stormers into the town with 2 divisions, Düpont's division staying in reserve outside. Soult's corps, the 4th, came from Ratzeburg: Legrand's division was charged with the advanced work of the Mühlen gate, which the Corsican tirailleurs and the tirailleurs du Pô carried while the 26th light, supported by the 18th and 75th of the line, scaled the rampart; Leval's division was directed on the Hertzberg gate and Saint-Hilaire's kept in reserve, and Soult wrote that the use of all these forces was not necessary. The Grand Duke of Berg names Grouchy's and d'Hautpoul's divisions, Lasalle's brigade, with which he marched in person with Soult, and Sahuc's division following. The 29th Bulletin has Drouet lead the 27th light and the 94th and 95th against the batteries.
claims.rationale: Bodart from the frame transcription, the rest read from the page images. The corps were brought up by the pursuit, but which of their troops were engaged was the commanders' choice (Dupont's and Saint-Hilaire's divisions in reserve, Rouyer's men at Schlutup), so the phase is left unresolved. Soult's corps is identified as the 4th by Foucart's footnote to his letter, which cites the 4th corps's report for the march from Ratzeburg. Höpfner's 'Düpont' and 'Rougere' are kept as printed. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; 'Marshal Bernadotte to the major general. Lübeck, 7 November 1806'; 'I ordered Drouet's division, which was at the head, to form by divisions and half-battalions and to advance, preceded by its voltigeur companies and supported by some pieces of cannon that I at once had placed on the'; 'during the attack on this last gate I had ordered General Rivaud to detach some companies to take a bastion placed on the left while I had it battered by 2 pieces of artillery'; 'Rivaud's division, debouching from the town into the country, met Legrand's division of Marshal Soult's corps'; 'Dupont's division stayed in reserve behind the town and was charged with watching the banks of the Trave, always ready to support the attack'; 'the 3 light cavalry regiments had also stayed there'; 'as soon as the town was in our power, I ordered General Tilly, who commanded them, to pass through it and debouch'; 'the 5th chasseur regiment went on the Travemünde road and the 2nd and 4th hussars on the Stockelsdorf road'; 'continuing our march we arrived at Schlutup, where we indeed saw on the Trave several ships ready to sail with Swedish troops, part of them already embarked, the others on the shore'; 'I charged General Rouyer, with part of his brigade, to make himself master of them'; 'Marshal Bernadotte left General Rougere there with a half-brigade and had some artillery set up in a bay of the Trave, which swept the river lengthwise, but himself continued the march on Lübeck'; 'thereby the Bellevue bastion was abandoned right after the storming of the Burgthor, and Marshal Bernadotte could at once follow the stormers into the town with 2 divisions and detach strong parties to open the Hörter and Mühlen gates to the troops of Marshal Soult and the Grand Duke of Berg'; 'Düpont's division remained in reserve outside the town'; 'Marshal Soult to the Emperor. Lübeck, 6 November 1806'; 'as I had the honour of reporting to Your Majesty in my last report, the army corps left Ratzeburg this morning before daylight and headed for Lübeck'; 'by following the left bank of the lake of Ratzeburg. (Report of the 4th corps.)'; 'General Legrand's division was charged with carrying the advanced work of the Mühlen gate'; 'the Corsican tirailleurs and the tirailleurs du Pô carried it with the bayonet after a resistance of an hour'; 'the 26th light infantry, supported by the 18th and 75th of the line, scaled the rampart at the same time, and the artillery broke in the gate'; 'General Leval's division was at the same time directed on the Hertzberg gate, which it was also to carry; that of General Saint-Hilaire was in reserve'; 'but the use of all these forces was not necessary'; 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor. Lübeck, 6 November 1806, 9 o'clock in the evening'; 'Grouchy's and d'Hautpoul's divisions appeared there at the same hour: the Prince of Ponte-Corvo by the Rehna road, Marshal Soult by the Ratzeburg road and the heavy cavalry by a road between the 2 army corps'; 'I marched in person with Marshal Soult and General Lasalle's brigade'; 'meanwhile Sahuc's division and the whole of Marshal Soult's corps were following; the various roads were intercepted; the rivers Wakenitz and Steckenitz were reconnoitred and observed'; '29th Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 9 November 1806'; 'General Drouet, at the head of the 27th light infantry and the 94th and 95th regiments, approached the batteries with the coolness and intrepidity that belong to French troops'.

claims.value: Höpfner: the three marshals, united at Schwerin, decided there on 4 November, given their superiority, to leave General Blücher no time to establish himself anywhere in a strong position; finding the position at Gadebusch abandoned on 5 November, Bernadotte followed directly by Rhena to Schönberg, while the Grand Duke of Berg and Soult turned left by Ratzeburg. Bernadotte wrote that he had agreed with Soult that Soult would march on Ratzeburg and he on Lübeck. Learning in the night that Swedes were about to embark, Bernadotte at once sent General Maison with some voltigeur companies, some guns and 100 horses to Schlutupp to interrupt the shipping on the Trave (Höpfner); at Schlutup he charged General Rouyer, with part of his brigade, to take the ships, then ordered him to sink them and throw troops onto the left bank to summon the Swedes (Bernadotte). Before Lübeck, though the enemy meant to defend the place and the ground gave him great advantages, Bernadotte did not hesitate to order the attack: Drouet's division, at the head, was to form by divisions and half-battalions and advance behind its voltigeurs, supported by guns; during the attack on the outer gate he ordered Rivaud to detach companies to take a bastion on the left; and once the town was taken he ordered Tilly to pass through it with the 3 light cavalry regiments and debouch. In Soult's corps Legrand's division was charged with the advanced work of the Mühlen gate, by Soult's order according to the Grand Duke of Berg, while Leval's division was directed on another gate and Saint-Hilaire's kept in reserve. The Grand Duke wrote that he marched in person with Soult and Lasalle's brigade, that he ordered the cavalry let through to pursue on the Travemünde road, and that d'Hautpoul had orders to summon Blücher. Soult wrote that the Grand Duke had principally directed the attacks; the Grand Duke, that no better dispositions could have been made than the marshals'. Höpfner: at the Mühlenthor, prisoners said that the Grand Duke commanded opposite.
claims.rationale: Side A's letters and side B's history, read from the page images. These were decisions taken in the action by side A's commanders, so the claim is tagged commander-created. The claim does not give the direction of the whole attack to one commander: Soult's and the Grand Duke's letters differ on it, and both are kept. English renderings (ours): 'the three marshals united at Schwerin had decided there on 4 November, given their superiority, to leave General Blücher no time to establish himself anywhere in a strong position'; 'when they therefore found the position at Gadebusch evacuated on 5 November and learned of the Prussians' retreat on Lübeck, Marshal Bernadotte followed at once directly from Gadebusch by Rhena to Schönberg, while the Grand Duke of Berg and Marshal Soult turned left by Ratzeburg'; 'Marshal Bernadotte to the major general. Lübeck, 7 November 1806'; 'I came to an understanding with Marshal Soult, and it was agreed that he would march on Ratzeburg and I on Lübeck'; 'still in the night to the 6th Marshal Bernadotte learned that a detachment of Swedes had withdrawn from Lauenburg to Lübeck and was about to embark at Travemünde'; 'he at once sent General Maison with some voltigeur companies, some guns and 100 horses to Schlutupp, with the order to interrupt the shipping on the Trave from there'; 'continuing our march we arrived at Schlutup, where we indeed saw on the Trave several ships ready to sail with Swedish troops, part of them already embarked, the others on the shore'; 'I charged General Rouyer, with part of his brigade, to make himself master of them'; 'but I ordered General Rouyer to sink the ships and at once throw some troops onto the left bank, summoning them to surrender if they did not want to be cut to pieces'; 'I soon recognised that the enemy meant to defend the place and that the locality gave him great advantages'; '[but, strong in the in]trepidity of our troops, I did not hesitate to order the attack'; 'I ordered Drouet's division, which was at the head, to form by divisions and half-battalions and to advance, preceded by its voltigeur companies and supported by some pieces of cannon that I at once had placed on the'; 'the inner gate was taken, but new resistance was met at the outer gate, which, like the rampart, was manned with infantry and defended by 2 pieces'; 'during the attack on this last gate I had ordered General Rivaud to detach some companies to take a bastion placed on the left while I had it battered by 2 pieces of artillery'; 'the 3 light cavalry regiments had also stayed there'; 'as soon as the town was in our power, I ordered General Tilly, who commanded them, to pass through it and debouch'; 'Marshal Soult to the Emperor. Lübeck, 6 November 1806'; 'General Legrand's division was charged with carrying the advanced work of the Mühlen gate'; 'General Leval's division was at the same time directed on the Hertzberg gate, which it was also to carry; that of General Saint-Hilaire was in reserve'; 'His Imperial and Royal Highness the Grand Duke of Berg, who principally directed the attacks and who had brought up his cavalry to take part in them'; 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor. Lübeck, 6 November 1806, 9 o'clock in the evening'; 'I marched in person with Marshal Soult and General Lasalle's brigade'; 'then General Legrand received Marshal Soult's order to attack the advanced works of the Mühlen gate'; 'then I ordered the cavalry to be let through, which pursued the enemy at sword's point on the Travemünde road, by which General Blücher withdrew'; 'General d'Hautpoul has the order to summon General Blücher'; 'it is impossible to make better dispositions than those the Marshals made'; 'the Mühlenthor was attacked first, early on the 6th, by Marshal Soult and the Grand Duke of Berg'; 'prisoners stated that the Grand Duke of Berg commanded opposite, and the presence of much cavalry confirmed it'.

claims.value: Höpfner: General Blücher would not fight at Gadebusch against the much superior enemy and decided to fall back on Lübeck, which the Duke of Brunswick-Oels was to take by goodwill or force. In Lübeck the regiments Manstein and Oels stood under the Duke of Oels, who was to command at the Burgthor; from there Blücher rode to the Hörter-Thor, where he handed the command to Colonel Görtzke of the regiment Owstien, showed him his position himself and gave him his instructions, and then to the Mühlenthor, where General Lettow commanded and all had orders to defend themselves to the utmost and think of no retreat; the other troops stood on other parts of the walls or in reserve in the town's squares under the commandant, General Natzmer. To a deputation of citizens asking him to leave the town Blücher answered that he would defend himself to the last man, and he forbade General Lettow's measure of burning the houses before the Mühlenthor. Towards noon the Duke of Oels, having sent to Blücher for support, ordered the fusiliers back into the town; there was then no reserve, no arrangement for closing the Burgthor and no commander there, since the Duke had had himself ferried to the Bellevue bastion for another horse, and when the enemy pressed up under that battery he ordered the 1st battalion of his regiment to march off. Outside the lost town Blücher hoped to attack it again in the night, then, hearing the defenders still firing at the Hörter and Mühlen gates, decided to attack at once with the regiment Kunheim under Colonel Thümen; the attack failed, and the retreat was taken towards the cavalry gathered behind Lübeck. At the Mühlenthor, at 2 in the afternoon, General Lettow had to have the chamade beaten.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images. These were side B's commanders' decisions in the action, so the claim is tagged commander-created. Where Höpfner says only 'the General' or 'he', the claim cites the sentence before or after it that names Blücher; the 'he' who ordered the fusiliers back is read as the Duke of Oels, the subject of the clause before it. English renderings (ours): 'General Blücher was therefore also not of the opinion that he should fight at Gadebusch with the greatly superior enemy, but believed that he must first reach a position in which the troops could be granted some rest in safety'; 'General Blücher therefore decided to go back to Lübeck'; 'the Duke of Brunswick-Oels was to take possession of the town by goodwill or by force'; 'on the curtain beside the Bellevue bastion stood the infantry regiment Manstein'; 'both this regiment and the regiment Oels stood under the command of the Duke of Oels, who was to command at the Burgthor'; 'from the Burgthor General Blücher rode to the Hörter-[Thor]'; '[Hörter-]Thor, where he handed the command to Colonel Görtzke, commander of the infantry regiment Owstien, showed him his position himself and gave him his instructions'; 'from the Hörterthor the General went to the Mühlenthor, where French cavalry had very early alarmed the troops still outside the gate'; 'there General Lettow commanded, with the regiment Tschammer on the wall right and left of the gate, and with the half grenadier battalion Rabiel, the rest of the regiment Winning, 100 riflemen of the regiment Kunheim, a company of the regiment Natzmer and several other collected men in a position before the gate, together with the regiment of Pletz hussars'; 'all had the order to defend themselves to the utmost and to think of no retreat'; 'all the other troops stood partly on other parts of the wall, partly in reserve in the squares of the town, under the command of the commandant, General Natzmer'; 'at half past eight a deputation of the citizenry had come to General Blücher to move him to leave the town, as he had promised the day before'; 'the General answered that circumstances had changed, that he had not believed the enemy so near; a withdrawal was therefore now no longer to be thought of; he would defend himself to the last man'; 'General Lettow had had the houses before the Mühlenthor cleared in order to set them on fire and thereby entirely hinder the enemy's attack for a long time, but General Blücher forbade this measure'; 'at last towards noon, after the Duke of Oels had already sent Lieutenant Stülpnagel of the regiment Oels on his own horse to General Blücher to ask for support, he ordered that the fusiliers should withdraw into the town, so that the artillery standing on the wall could fire freely'; 'in the Burgthor there stood no reserve, nor had any arrangement been made to close the gate, nor was there a commander who might have given orders for the defence, since the Duke, who had taken part in the last part of the action on foot, had at once had himself ferried in a boat to the Bellevue bastion to get another riding horse there'; 'the artillery on the Bellevue bastion had at first worked powerfully with canister against the following enemy during the action at the Burgthor, and so for the moment at least prevented a pressing-on in great masses; but when the enemy, skirmishing, pushed up under the battery, the Duke of Oels ordered that the 1st battalion of his regiment should march off and leave only a detachment with the artillery'; 'General Blücher lost with Lübeck a great part of his artillery, 22 guns without the regimental cannon, and the main strength of the infantry'; 'outside the town General Blücher found the Duke of Oels and General Natzmer already there'; 'despite the unfavourable circumstances the General conceived the hope of being able to attack Lübeck again with success in the following night, and this hope calmed him for the moment'; 'but hardly had he moved a little away from the town with the rescued infantry when he heard the very lively fire of the troops still defending themselves at the Hörter and Mühlen gates'; 'this brought him to the decision to risk another attack on Lübeck at once'; 'the regiment Kunheim had to face about, form columns of sections and go forward to the attack under the leadership of the brave Colonel Thümen'; 'the superiority was however too great, and when the bridge at the gate was now also occupied by the French, the Prussians were fired on most heavily in front and flanks'; 'the retreat had to be taken towards the cavalry gathered behind Lübeck'; 'the men were almost all dead or wounded, the cartridges all fired off, in the town the fighting had long since stopped, when at last at 2 o'clock in the afternoon General Lettow had to have the chamade beaten'.

claims.value: Bodart codes the engagement at Lübeck on 6 November 1806 as a victory of the French under Marshals Bernadotte and Soult over the Prussians under Blücher. Höpfner: General Blücher had to fight his way out of the town and lost with Lübeck a great part of his artillery and the main strength of his infantry; at half past three Lübeck was wholly in French hands. Soult wrote that Legrand forced the Mühlen gate as the 1st corps entered the town from another side; the Grand Duke of Berg, that the Prince of Ponte-Corvo had the same success at the Burgen gate, that the heads of the 2 corps met in the middle of the town, and that the cavalry pursued the enemy on the Travemünde road, by which Blücher withdrew.

claims.value: Side B's loss in the reports, kept apart. Bernadotte: the day's results were nearly 3,000 killed or wounded, more than 5,000 prisoners including the Swedes, 10 flags, 2 standards and more than 30 guns; his account counts the convoy of 300 wagons and its escort of about 1,000 infantry and 2 squadrons of hussars, who all laid down their arms, the 2 guns and 1,200 prisoners taken at the outer gate, 500 men and 2 guns in the bastion on the left, 4 squadrons cut off by the 2nd and 4th hussars that surrendered to the Grand Duke of Berg's cavalry, a battalion made to lay down its arms, a whole squadron taken by the 5th chasseurs, 500 more prisoners at Schwartau, and 2,000 prisoners disputed between Legrand's and Rivaud's divisions. Soult: 1,500 prisoners with their officers and 2 generals in the attack on the Mühlen gate, 4 Prussian squadrons cut off with their guns that capitulated, and for the day at least 6,000 prisoners, 50 guns, several flags and standards, 3 generals and much baggage; the 4th corps's report in Foucart's footnotes gives Legrand's division 2,500 prisoners with their officers and 2 generals, 9 flags and 25 guns with their caissons, has the light cavalry take the surrender of 3 squadrons of Prussian dragoons with 4 guns near Fackenburg, and has the cavalry pick up the equivalent of a battalion at Padelügge. The Grand Duke of Berg: a guidon and 200 mounted men taken before the town, 1,200 men and 3 generals in the advanced works, a column of 6 squadrons and some battalions, withdrawn by the Hamburg road, that surrendered to Soult's light cavalry, and for the day 5,000 men, 3 or 4 generals and at least 50 guns. The 29th Bulletin: 4,000 prisoners, 60 guns, several generals and a great number of officers killed or taken, and the convoy of 300 wagons. Höpfner: General Blücher lost with Lübeck 22 guns without the regimental cannon and the main strength of his infantry; the regiment Tschammer alone lost about 300 men, and the rest of the regiment Owstien surrendered after very great loss; about 4000 wounded had to be cared for and 5—6000 prisoners were lodged in the churches; behind Krempelsdorf Major Ende's capitulation handed over about 360 more horses and 4 horse guns, and Major Witzleben's 4 companies, still 9 officers and 136 men, were overwhelmed; the baggage sent to Wismar under Captain Froideville was taken on the march; and in the night the enemy surprised Schwartau and took most of the regiment Kunheim at the bridge. The Swedish detachment at Schlutup, not Prussian, is given apart: more than 600 prisoners (Bernadotte), 1,000 or 1,200 already embarked (the Grand Duke of Berg), 1,600 (the Bulletin).
claims.rationale: Separate accounts read from the page images, not combined. They overlap and count different things: the Grand Duke's 1,200 in the advanced works and Soult's 1,500 in the Mühlen-gate attack may be the same men, Legrand's 2,500 fall within Soult's 6,000, Bernadotte's 5,000 include the Swedes, and Höpfner does not say whose wounded his 4000 were. The passages read do not establish whether Major Ende's capitulation is the surrender of the 3 dragoon squadrons with 4 guns or of the 4 squadrons with their guns, nor whether Bernadotte's 500 at Schwartau are the regiment Kunheim's men. The 4th corps's 2,500 (the OCR reads 600) and 25, and its 3 squadrons, were checked on full-resolution crops. The 29th Bulletin's 16,000 prisoners cover Lübeck and Ratkau together and are not split; Ratkau is B376b. English renderings (ours): 'Marshal Bernadotte to the major general. Lübeck, 7 November 1806'; 'the results of the day are nearly 3,000 men killed or wounded, more than 5,000 prisoners including the Swedes, 10 flags, 2 standards and more than 30 pieces of cannon'; 'arrived at Selmsdorf, I and my escort were charged by the enemy hussars'; 'I had 1 battalion of Drouet's division advance, preceded by some voltigeurs, and soon we had in our power a convoy of 300 baggage wagons escorted by about 1,000 infantry and 2 squadrons of hussars, who all laid down their arms'; 'the inner gate was taken, but new resistance was met at the outer gate, which, like the rampart, was manned with infantry and defended by 2 pieces'; 'there were taken besides the 2 pieces and 1,200 prisoners'; 'during the attack on this last gate I had ordered General Rivaud to detach some companies to take a bastion placed on the left while I had it battered by 2 pieces of artillery'; '500 men and 2 pieces of cannon were taken there'; 'the 5th chasseur regiment went on the Travemünde road and the 2nd and 4th hussars on the Stockelsdorf road'; 'the 2nd and 4th cut off 4 enemy squadrons, which surrendered to the cavalry of the Grand Duke of Berg, which had just debouched immediately after mine'; 'they then made a battalion lay down its arms'; 'the 5th, heading for Travemünde, where the main body of the enemy had withdrawn, charged part of its rearguard and took a whole squadron'; 'Rivaud's and Drouet's divisions, having continued their march on Schwartau, drove the enemy out of it and took 500 more prisoners from him'; 'a dispute arose between Legrand's division and Rivaud's division over 2,000 prisoners who, pursued by General Rivaud's troops, threw themselves on those of General Legrand'; 'continuing our march we arrived at Schlutup, where we indeed saw on the Trave several ships ready to sail with Swedish troops, part of them already embarked, the others on the shore'; 'more than 600 Swedes surrendered as prisoners of war, under the orders of Colonel Count de Meurner'; 'Marshal Soult to the Emperor. Lübeck, 6 November 1806'; 'General Legrand's division was charged with carrying the advanced work of the Mühlen gate'; '1,500 prisoners with their officers and 2 generals were taken in this attack'; 'as soon as the cavalry could debouch, that of the army corps set off in pursuit of the enemy'; 'in its first movement it cut off 4 Prussian squadrons with their guns. After a slight resistance, they capitulated'; 'this day yields at least 6,000 prisoners, 50 cannon, several flags and standards, 3 generals and a considerable amount of baggage'; 'Legrand's division took on the ramparts of the town, at the outworks and in the streets 2,500 prisoners with their officers and 2 generals (Generals Haufberg and Zwiffel); it took 9 flags and 25 pieces of cannon with their caissons'; 'Adjutant-commandant Cosson, his chief of staff, and his own aides-de-camp. (4th corps.)'; 'the light cavalry of the army corps, having gone towards Fackenburg, a Danish village, met 3 squadrons of Prussian dragoons with 4 pieces of cannon who, unable to get through by Holstein, had their retreat cut off and surrendered after making some efforts (useless, in truth) to open a way'; 'the cavalry of His Highness the Grand Duke of Berg and that of the 1st corps took the Travemünde road. (4th corps.)'; 'the cavalry was posted in the village of Padelügge, where it picked up the equivalent of an enemy battalion that had been cut off. (4th corps.)'; 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor. Lübeck, 6 November 1806, 9 o'clock in the evening'; 'Marshal Soult's light troops and the Lasalle brigade met the enemy a league in front of the town, charged him, overthrew him, carried off a guidon and took 200 mounted men'; 'then General Legrand received Marshal Soult's order to attack the advanced works of the Mühlen gate'; '1,200 men and 3 generals who defended them were made prisoner'; 'a column that had withdrawn by the Hamburg road, 6 squadrons and some battalions strong, surrendered to Marshal Soult's light cavalry'; 'Sire, 5,000 men, 3 or 4 generals, at least 50 pieces of cannon were the results of this day'; 'the Prince of Ponte-Corvo took 1,000 or 1,200 Swedes who were already embarked'; '29th Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 9 November 1806'; 'arrived at Schlutup on the Trave, he had a corps of 1,600 Swedes surrounded, who had at last judged it fitting to carry out their retreat from the Lauenburg to embark on the Trave'; 'a convoy of 300 wagons, which General Savary had pursued from Wismar, was enveloped by the Prince of Ponte-Corvo's column and taken'; '4,000 prisoners, 60 pieces of cannon, several generals, a great number of officers killed or taken, such is the result of this fine day'; 'these 2 days destroyed the last corps that remained of the Prussian army, and won us the rest of the artillery of that army, many flags and 16,000 prisoners, among whom are 4,000 men of cavalry'; 'General Blücher lost with Lübeck a great part of his artillery, 22 guns without the regimental cannon, and the main strength of the infantry'; 'the regiment Tschammer alone had a loss of about 300 men'; 'when the Mühlenthor had been opened, cavalry broke into the town; the regiment Owstien formed square, and only after very great loss did the rest of the regiment and the Jäger and fusiliers who had fled to it have to surrender'; 'about 4000 wounded had to be cared for, 5—6000 prisoners lodged in the churches, to whom only boiled flour, black bread and straw were handed through the windows'; 'the fire of the horse artillery was stopped and an officer with a trumpeter sent forward and taken to Colonel Ricaud, aide of Marshal Soult, who brought Major Ende behind Krempelsdorf to the Grand Duke of Berg, Marshal Bernadotte and Marshal Soult'; 'the capitulation was soon concluded and about 360 more horses and 4 horse guns handed over to the enemy, after the squadron posted at Hambergen had also come up'; 'Major Witzleben, who had already partly destroyed the bridge at Moisling, was disturbed in this work by the enemy cavalry that had crossed at Krumeß and Kronsvoer, and soon afterwards also attacked by enemy infantry'; 'on this march he was unexpectedly attacked from a garden wall on the left by a considerable mass of enemy infantry and in front by cavalry, and overwhelmed before the guns could even unlimber'; 'the 4 companies were still 9 officers 136 men strong'; 'on the march the part of the Prussian baggage that had been sent on 3 November from Dobbertin to Wismar under Captain Froideville was overtaken and taken by the French troops'; 'while in Ratkau, at General Blücher's headquarters, the necessary arrangements for the following day were still being made, the report came in that the enemy had surprised Schwartau and taken the troops posted there prisoner'; 'hardly had this happened when the enemy, under cover of the dark, rainy night, attacked the dragoon posts with the greatest violence'; 'so the enemy, pressing on fast, was able to scatter everything in the darkness and take most of the regiment Kunheim prisoner at the bridge in the village'.

claims.value: Side A's loss in the reports: Bernadotte estimated his corps's loss at more than 1,500 killed or wounded, with several companies now commanded only by their sergeant-major and many brave officers to regret, and at the outer gate the 8th regiment had already lost many men. The 4th corps's report says the loss of Legrand's division was not very considerable. The Grand Duke of Berg wrote that Lasalle, received under the walls by 6 rounds of canister, lost some men. Höpfner says the Prussian artillery at the Mühlenthor inflicted great losses on the enemy. No passage read gives a figure for Soult's corps or the cavalry, or a total for side A other than Bodart's about 2,000.
claims.rationale: Side A's letters and side B's history, read from the page images, with Bodart from the frame transcription; the 1,500 was checked on a full-resolution crop. Bernadotte's 'our loss' is read as his corps's, the subject of his letter. Bodart's about 2,000 (claim bodart-losses) is above Bernadotte's figure. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-losses; 'Marshal Bernadotte to the major general. Lübeck, 7 November 1806'; 'this day was one of the most brilliant that can be cited; but Your Highness will understand that it must also have been very bloody; we have to regret many brave officers'; 'I estimate our loss at more than 1,500 men killed or wounded; several companies are now commanded only by their sergeant-major'; 'the inner gate was taken, but new resistance was met at the outer gate, which, like the rampart, was manned with infantry and defended by 2 pieces'; 'the 8th regiment had already lost many men without anything being able to shake its ardour'; 'Marshal Soult to the Emperor. Lübeck, 6 November 1806'; 'Legrand's division took on the ramparts of the town, at the outworks and in the streets 2,500 prisoners with their officers and 2 generals (Generals Haufberg and Zwiffel); it took 9 flags and 25 pieces of cannon with their caissons'; 'through the effect of the wise dispositions that General Legrand made and the rare intrepidity the men showed, their loss was not very considerable'; 'Adjutant-commandant Cosson, his chief of staff, and his own aides-de-camp. (4th corps.)'; 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor. Lübeck, 6 November 1806, 9 o'clock in the evening'; 'General Lasalle, carrying through his charge, arrived under the walls of the town, where he was received by 6 rounds of canister; he lost some men and kept his position'; 'the Mühlenthor was attacked first, early on the 6th, by Marshal Soult and the Grand Duke of Berg'; 'at last a lively attack followed, in which the cannonade became very heavy; the enemy however had to give up his purpose, since the Prussian artillery at the Mühlenthor, supported by that at the Hörterthor, was very superior and inflicted great losses on the enemy'.

claims.value: Bodart places Lübeck, a free city of northern Germany, on the Trave, 15 km from the Baltic. Höpfner: the town lay on the right bank of the Trave at the inflow of the Wakenitz; on the German side it had 3 gates, the Burgthor, where the roads from Gadebusch by Herrenburg, from Schlutupp and from Travemünde met, the Mühlenthor, which took the roads from Ratzeburg and Hamburg, and the Hörter-Thor between them; on the left bank only the Holstein gate led to Danish territory; and on this stretch the Trave could be crossed only on bridges. Before the Burgthor the ground rose towards the Galgenberg and overlooked the gate and the half-circle work before it, whose approach was a causeway 20 paces wide between the water of the broad Wakenitz and the deep Trave, flanked for 200 paces by the Bellevue bastion beyond the Trave. Bernadotte wrote that the town was surrounded by marshes, that on his side a lake covered its whole front, and that all his troops had to file along a causeway leading to the gate. The 1st corps journal, in Foucart's footnote: Lübeck lies in a plain, marshy in places, whose accidents do not give the attacker great advantages for placing his artillery; the roads from Schönberg and Travemünde meet at the gate at right angles, bordered by deep ditches, gardens, trees and houses, and the ground between them is entirely marshy, though passable in places.
claims.rationale: Bodart's locator and the descriptions, read from the page images (Bodart's from the frame transcription). The ground was there before the action, so the claim is tagged inherited. The journal's description is in Foucart's footnote 1 to Bernadotte's letter, which closes with '(Journal du 1er corps.)'. Höpfner's 'Halbzirkel' is rendered 'half-circle'. English renderings (ours): Bodart, '(free city in northern Germany, on the Trave, 15 km from the Baltic)'; 'the town of Lübeck, on the right bank of the Trave at the inflow of the Wakenitz, had in earlier times a bastioned main wall with wet ditches, which were fed by the Trave and the Wakenitz'; 'the German side, or the enclosure on the right bank of the Trave, had 3 gates: the Burgthor, in which the roads from Gadebusch by Herrenburg, from Schlutupp and from Travemünde by the Herren-Fähre met; the Mühlenthor, which took the roads from Ratzeburg and from Hamburg; and the Hörter-Thor between them'; 'on the left bank of the Trave only the Holstein gate led to Danish territory'; 'it still had wall and ditch, and if it were properly defended, the infantry posted along the Trave on Lübeck and Swedish territory, the cavalry could recover behind it, the infantry also be properly fed, and since the enemy needed some days to pass the Trave, which on this stretch can be crossed only on bridges, the General could accept the fight under very favourable circumstances'; 'to this unpleasant position was added that the ground before the Burgthor rose towards the Galgenberg and fully overlooked the gate and the half-circle'; 'the approach to the half-circle was formed by a causeway 20 paces wide, bounded on both sides by the water of the broad Wakenitz and the deep Trave for 100 paces from the half-circle'; 'the Bellevue bastion, lying beyond the Trave, flanked the causeway for 200 paces with artillery and musket fire'; 'Marshal Bernadotte to the major general. Lübeck, 7 November 1806'; 'the town is surrounded by marshes, and on our side a lake covered its whole front'; 'to reach it all the troops had to file along a causeway that leads to the gate of the town'; 'Lübeck is in the middle of a plain, marshy in certain places, and the accidents of the ground are not considerable enough to give the attacker great advantages for placing his artillery'; 'the two roads from Schönberg and from Travemünde join at the gate at right angles to each other; they are bordered by fairly deep ditches, gardens, trees and houses'; 'the ground between the two is entirely marshy, though passable in some places. (Journal of the 1st corps.)'.

claims.value: Side B (Prussian), in Höpfner: at Gadebusch the army still had numerous cavalry, but with very worn horses, and about 100 guns, but only the 1st corps had enough ammunition; the infantry lacked shoes, so that most had already walked their feet sore; money, bread and forage were lacking, the country around Gadebusch could not quickly make good the want, and there was no baggage. General Blücher had sent Rittmeister Bardeleben to Hamburg to raise a loan of 100,000 Reichsthaler to pay the troops. Lübeck, a rich trading town, offered money, food and shoes in plenty. In the town a hussar officer clearing the streets of vehicles also sent back the artillery's ammunition wagons in the half-circle before the Burgthor, so that the half battery of 12-pounders had for the moment only the 3 rounds of canister in the trail boxes; later the wagons were brought back to the nearest work, still at a considerable distance. At the Mühlenthor the cartridges were all fired off before the chamade. No passage read describes side A's supply.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images; the ½ and the 3 were checked on full-resolution crops. The passages mix the state brought from the retreat with events in the action, so the phase is left unresolved. Höpfner's '½ — 12pfündige Batterie' is read as a half battery of 12-pounders. English renderings (ours): 'the army had lost perhaps 4—5000 men on the retreat through fights, desertion and men worn out; it still had, it is true, numerous cavalry, but with very exhausted horses, counted about 100 guns, but only the 1st corps had sufficient ammunition'; 'the infantry lacked shoes, so that most had already walked their feet sore'; 'there was a want of money, of bread and forage, and the country around Gadebusch was not suited to make good quickly what was lacking; there was a want of baggage'; 'General Blücher was therefore also not of the opinion that he should fight at Gadebusch with the greatly superior enemy, but believed that he must first reach a position in which the troops could be granted some rest in safety'; 'the inspection adjutant, Rittmeister Bardeleben, had been sent by General Blücher to Hamburg to raise a loan of 100,000 Reichsthaler for the payment of the soldiers' pay'; 'the latter place was the nearest, only 5 miles away, was like Hamburg a rich trading [town]'; '[trading] town, in which all needs in money, food, shoes etc. were found in plenty'; 'hardly were the guns set up when a hussar officer, who had the order to clear the streets of the mass of vehicles, also sent back the artillery's ammunition wagons in the half-circle, so that the half 12-pounder battery had for the moment for its guns only the 3 rounds of canister in the trail boxes'; 'only later did they succeed in bringing the ammunition wagons back to the work nearest the post, but still at a considerable distance'; 'to this unpleasant position was added that the ground before the Burgthor rose towards the Galgenberg and fully overlooked the gate and the half-circle'; 'they defended themselves at the Mühlenthor, thus attacked in the right flank, front and rear, under General Lettow like desperate men, although the enemy had occupied the houses behind the walls, uncovered the roofs and fired on the defenders most heavily from there'; 'the men were almost all dead or wounded, the cartridges all fired off, in the town the fighting had long since stopped, when at last at 2 o'clock in the afternoon General Lettow had to have the chamade beaten'.

claims.value: At Schönberg at 4 in the morning of the 6th Bernadotte wrote to the Grand Duke of Berg that all the reports and reconnaissances gave him the certainty that the enemy had not made the suspected turn towards Wismar and had very few men at Lübeck. His letter of 7 November says that his reconnaissances had told him that Blücher had directed part of his troops on Lübeck while another column took the Ratzeburg road, and that in the night he learned that 2,000 Swedes retreating from the Lauenburg had entered Lübeck and were to embark on the Trave; Höpfner has the marshals find the Gadebusch position abandoned on 5 November and learn of the Prussians' retreat on Lübeck, and Bernadotte learn of the Swedes in the night to the 6th. Before the town Bernadotte soon recognised that the enemy meant to defend it and that the locality gave him great advantages. The Grand Duke of Berg wrote that the rivers Wakenitz and Steckenitz were reconnoitred and observed.
claims.rationale: Side A's letters and side B's history, read from the page images; the 2,000 was checked on a full-resolution crop. Bernadotte's morning estimate stands against the larger figures in his own letter of the 7th and in the journal (claim side-b-strength-french). English renderings (ours): 'Marshal Bernadotte to the Grand Duke of Berg. Schönberg, 6 November 1806, 4 o'clock in the morning'; 'all the reports that have reached me and the result of the reconnaissances I sent out give me the certainty that the enemy has not made the hook towards Wismar that we suspected, and that he has very few men at Lübeck'; 'Marshal Bernadotte to the major general. Lübeck, 7 November 1806'; 'since then my reconnaissances told me that General Blücher had indeed directed part of his troops on Lübeck, but that at the same time another column had taken the road to Ratzeburg'; 'during the night I learned that 2,000 Swedes retreating from the Lauenburg had entered Lübeck yesterday and were to embark there on the Trave'; 'when they therefore found the position at Gadebusch evacuated on 5 November and learned of the Prussians' retreat on Lübeck, Marshal Bernadotte followed at once directly from Gadebusch by Rhena to Schönberg, while the Grand Duke of Berg and Marshal Soult turned left by Ratzeburg'; 'still in the night to the 6th Marshal Bernadotte learned that a detachment of Swedes had withdrawn from Lauenburg to Lübeck and was about to embark at Travemünde'; 'I soon recognised that the enemy meant to defend the place and that the locality gave him great advantages'; 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor. Lübeck, 6 November 1806, 9 o'clock in the evening'; 'meanwhile Sahuc's division and the whole of Marshal Soult's corps were following; the various roads were intercepted; the rivers Wakenitz and Steckenitz were reconnoitred and observed'.

claims.value: Höpfner: the Elbe crossing at Lauenburg had been given up, by some accounts because of news that some thousands of enemy cavalry already blocked the way. At half past eight General Blücher told a deputation of citizens that circumstances had changed and that he had not believed the enemy so near. At the Mühlenthor prisoners said that the Grand Duke of Berg commanded opposite, and the presence of much cavalry confirmed it; Blücher stayed mostly at the Mühlenthor, where he had expected the main attack. After the Burgthor fell, Captain Müffling pointed out to him that he was already cut off from the Holstein gate; outside the town the Duke of Oels said he had not known that the General was still in the town, and General Natzmer that, as he was about to advance to the Burgthor in support, the routed Prussian troops and the enemy's were already coming at him. In the night, while orders for the next day were being given at Ratkau, the report came that the enemy had surprised Schwartau and taken the troops there prisoner.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images. The sentence at the head of p. 292 begins on p. 291, which was not transcribed; its 'him' is read as Blücher from the sentences that follow ('the General ...'; 'outside the town General Blücher found ...'). The report of Schwartau's surprise came in the night, at Ratkau, after the town was lost. English renderings (ours): 'the Elbe crossing at Lauenburg was given up; according to some statements, because there was news that the way there had already been blocked by some thousands of enemy cavalry'; 'at half past eight a deputation of the citizenry had come to General Blücher to move him to leave the town, as he had promised the day before'; 'the General answered that circumstances had changed, that he had not believed the enemy so near; a withdrawal was therefore now no longer to be thought of; he would defend himself to the last man'; 'the Mühlenthor was attacked first, early on the 6th, by Marshal Soult and the Grand Duke of Berg'; 'prisoners stated that the Grand Duke of Berg commanded opposite, and the presence of much cavalry confirmed it'; 'General Blücher, who had stayed mostly at the Mühlenthor, where he had expected the main attack, had, after'; 'and to withdraw to the Holstein gate, when Captain Müffling pointed out to him that he was already cut off from there, since the fire at the Trave bridge, which was still defended by light troops, had grown ever livelier'; 'the General now had to fight his way out of the town in earnest and was fired on from every cross street on the way'; 'outside the town General Blücher found the Duke of Oels and General Natzmer already there'; 'the Duke replied that he had not known that the General was still in the town, and General Natzmer said that at the moment he had wanted to advance towards the Burgthor in support, the routed troops of his own side and the enemy's were already coming towards him'; 'while in Ratkau, at General Blücher's headquarters, the necessary arrangements for the following day were still being made, the report came in that the enemy had surprised Schwartau and taken the troops posted there prisoner'.

claims.value: Höpfner: the three marshals decided at Schwerin on 4 November, given their superiority, to leave General Blücher no time to establish himself anywhere in a strong position. Bernadotte sent General Maison to Schlutupp to interrupt the shipping on the Trave (Höpfner) and charged General Rouyer to take the Swedish ships (his letter). On the evening of the 6th the Grand Duke of Berg wrote that he hoped the result would be the capture of General Blücher's whole corps and the Duke of Weimar's, that at daybreak all the cavalry would march on Blücher, and that d'Hautpoul had orders to summon him; Soult, that the remainder of Blücher's column and General Wenniping's, which had withdrawn towards Travemünde, would be pursued there the next day and no doubt forced to surrender unless it broke through the cordon of Danish troops on the Holstein frontier.
claims.rationale: Side A's letters and side B's history, read from the page images. These were the marshals' own aims in the pursuit and the action, so the claim is tagged commander-created; no order from above for the attack on Lübeck was read. 'Wenniping' is printed so in Foucart and kept. English renderings (ours): 'the three marshals united at Schwerin had decided there on 4 November, given their superiority, to leave General Blücher no time to establish himself anywhere in a strong position'; 'still in the night to the 6th Marshal Bernadotte learned that a detachment of Swedes had withdrawn from Lauenburg to Lübeck and was about to embark at Travemünde'; 'he at once sent General Maison with some voltigeur companies, some guns and 100 horses to Schlutupp, with the order to interrupt the shipping on the Trave from there'; 'Marshal Bernadotte to the major general. Lübeck, 7 November 1806'; 'continuing our march we arrived at Schlutup, where we indeed saw on the Trave several ships ready to sail with Swedish troops, part of them already embarked, the others on the shore'; 'I charged General Rouyer, with part of his brigade, to make himself master of them'; 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor. Lübeck, 6 November 1806, 9 o'clock in the evening'; 'Sire, I hasten to announce to Your Majesty the most brilliant success, the result of which will be, I hope, the capture of the whole corps of General Blücher and that of the Duke of Weimar'; 'tomorrow at daybreak all the cavalry will march on General Blücher'; 'General d'Hautpoul has the order to summon General Blücher'; 'Marshal Soult to the Emperor. Lübeck, 6 November 1806'; 'the remainder of General Blücher's column and that of General Wenniping, united, withdrew towards Travemünde'; 'tomorrow it will be pursued there and no doubt forced to surrender, unless it forces the cordon of Danish troops on the Holstein frontier'.

claims.value: Höpfner: General Blücher would not fight at Gadebusch but sought first a position where the troops could be given some rest in safety. Of the two directions left, Hamburg and Lübeck, Lübeck was the nearer, a rich trading town with plenty of money, food and shoes; it still had wall and ditch, and if it were properly defended, with the infantry along the Trave on Lübeck and Swedish territory, the cavalry could recover behind it and the infantry be fed, and since the enemy needed some days to cross the Trave, the General could accept battle in very favourable circumstances; reinforcement by the Swedish troops that had withdrawn to Lübeck to embark at Travemünde was also counted on. In Lübeck Blücher told the citizens' deputation that he would defend himself to the last man, and at the Mühlenthor all had orders to defend themselves to the utmost and think of no retreat. When the town was lost he hoped to attack it again in the night, then decided to attack at once.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images. These were Blücher's own aims, so the claim is tagged commander-created. Where Höpfner says only 'the General' or 'he', the claim cites the sentence that names Blücher. English renderings (ours): 'General Blücher was therefore also not of the opinion that he should fight at Gadebusch with the greatly superior enemy, but believed that he must first reach a position in which the troops could be granted some rest in safety'; 'there remained next only two directions: to Hamburg or to Lübeck'; 'the latter place was the nearest, only 5 miles away, was like Hamburg a rich trading [town]'; '[trading] town, in which all needs in money, food, shoes etc. were found in plenty'; 'it still had wall and ditch, and if it were properly defended, the infantry posted along the Trave on Lübeck and Swedish territory, the cavalry could recover behind it, the infantry also be properly fed, and since the enemy needed some days to pass the Trave, which on this stretch can be crossed only on bridges, the General could accept the fight under very favourable circumstances'; 'it was also counted on to see the army reinforced by the Swedish troops, which had withdrawn from the Lauenburg country to Lübeck to be embarked at Travemünde'; 'General Blücher therefore decided to go back to Lübeck'; 'at half past eight a deputation of the citizenry had come to General Blücher to move him to leave the town, as he had promised the day before'; 'the General answered that circumstances had changed, that he had not believed the enemy so near; a withdrawal was therefore now no longer to be thought of; he would defend himself to the last man'; 'from the Hörterthor the General went to the Mühlenthor, where French cavalry had very early alarmed the troops still outside the gate'; 'all had the order to defend themselves to the utmost and to think of no retreat'; 'General Blücher lost with Lübeck a great part of his artillery, 22 guns without the regimental cannon, and the main strength of the infantry'; 'despite the unfavourable circumstances the General conceived the hope of being able to attack Lübeck again with success in the following night, and this hope calmed him for the moment'; 'but hardly had he moved a little away from the town with the rescued infantry when he heard the very lively fire of the troops still defending themselves at the Hörter and Mühlen gates'; 'this brought him to the decision to risk another attack on Lübeck at once'.

claims.value: Side A (French) attacked the town held by side B. Bernadotte, seeing that the enemy meant to defend it, ordered the attack, with Drouet's division at the head; on the other side Soult's light artillery was placed 100 toises from the place and the enemy attacked at once, and Legrand's division carried the advanced work and forced the Mühlen gate; Höpfner has the Mühlenthor attacked first, early on the 6th, by Soult and the Grand Duke of Berg. The 29th Bulletin: the enemy thought he could gain a day there, but to see him, reconnoitre him and attack him was the affair of an instant. Side B defended the walls and gates; after the Burgthor fell, General Blücher counter-attacked with the regiment Kunheim to within 100 paces of the Holstein gate and was driven back.
claims.rationale: Coded A_attacked: all the accounts read have side A attack the town and its gates and side B defend them. Tagged commander-created: the attack followed the marshals' decision of 4 November to leave Blücher no time and Bernadotte's own order on seeing the defences (claim side-a-command). English renderings (ours): 'Marshal Bernadotte to the major general. Lübeck, 7 November 1806'; 'I soon recognised that the enemy meant to defend the place and that the locality gave him great advantages'; '[but, strong in the in]trepidity of our troops, I did not hesitate to order the attack'; 'I ordered Drouet's division, which was at the head, to form by divisions and half-battalions and to advance, preceded by its voltigeur companies and supported by some pieces of cannon that I at once had placed on the'; 'Marshal Soult to the Emperor. Lübeck, 6 November 1806'; 'as soon as the light artillery had arrived, it was placed 100 toises from the place and the works, and the enemy was attacked at once'; 'General Legrand's division was charged with carrying the advanced work of the Mühlen gate'; 'General Legrand forced the Mühlen gate and entered the town at the same time as the 1st army corps was entering it from another side'; 'the Mühlenthor was attacked first, early on the 6th, by Marshal Soult and the Grand Duke of Berg'; 'the three marshals united at Schwerin had decided there on 4 November, given their superiority, to leave General Blücher no time to establish himself anywhere in a strong position'; '29th Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 9 November 1806'; 'the enemy had hastily arranged the old enceinte of Lübeck; he had placed batteries on the bastions; he did not doubt that he could gain a day there; but to see him, reconnoitre him and attack him was the affair of an instant'; 'the gates are at once broken in, the bastions scaled, the enemy put to flight, and the Prince of Ponte-Corvo's corps enters by the Trave gate'; 'General Blücher lost with Lübeck a great part of his artillery, 22 guns without the regimental cannon, and the main strength of the infantry'; 'this brought him to the decision to risk another attack on Lübeck at once'; 'the regiment Kunheim had to face about, form columns of sections and go forward to the attack under the leadership of the brave Colonel Thümen'; 'he pressed forward, accompanied by Generals Blücher and Natzmer and the Duke of Oels, at a slow pace with determination to within 100 paces of the Holstein gate, despite the heavy flanking fire from the walls'; 'the superiority was however too great, and when the bridge at the gate was now also occupied by the French, the Prussians were fired on most heavily in front and flanks'; 'the retreat had to be taken towards the cavalry gathered behind Lübeck'.

claims.value: Side B held a fortified town. Höpfner: Lübeck had in earlier times a bastioned main wall with wet ditches fed by the Trave and the Wakenitz; the parapets had begun to be removed, but the walls and ditches were still fully sufficient to repulse a storm. The 1st corps journal, in Foucart's footnote: the bastioned enceinte was dismantled, but the terre-pleins and the ditches, at least 10 feet deep, in which the Trave and the Wakenitz flow, had been kept, and in place of the former demi-lune a tambour of spaced palisades on a retaining wall had been built. Bernadotte wrote that the Prussians had made the gate a veritable place d'armes, bristling with cannon, with guns on 2 bastions on the flanks of the entrance; the 29th Bulletin, that the enemy was fortifying himself at Lübeck and had hastily arranged its old enceinte and placed batteries on the bastions. At the Hörter-Thor two horse guns were posted about 200 paces ahead and secured against cavalry by felled trees, and the 4 battalion pieces stood on the broken-down powder tower (Höpfner). Soult wrote of the advanced work of the Mühlen gate and of a kind of hornwork, entirely detached and defended by 2 battalions, that was also forced.
claims.rationale: Coded B_fortified: the walls, ditches and gates were permanent works held by side B at the start, so the claim is tagged inherited; the batteries and the felled trees were side B's preparations before the attack. All the accounts read have side A storm works that side B held. English renderings (ours): 'the town of Lübeck, on the right bank of the Trave at the inflow of the Wakenitz, had in earlier times a bastioned main wall with wet ditches, which were fed by the Trave and the Wakenitz'; 'at the time the parapets had begun to be removed, but the walls and ditches were still fully sufficient to repulse a storm'; 'Marshal Bernadotte to the major general. Lübeck, 7 November 1806'; 'the town formerly had a bastioned enceinte; it is dismantled, but the terre-pleins have been kept, as well as the ditches, at least 10 feet deep, in which the Trave and the Wakenitz flow'; 'in place of the demi-lune that once existed, a tambour has been built of spaced palisades set on a retaining wall and closed by a barrier like the enceinte'; 'the ground between the two is entirely marshy, though passable in some places. (Journal of the 1st corps.)'; 'the Prussians had made this gate a veritable place d'armes'; 'it bristled with cannon, and 2 bastions placed on the flanks of the entrance had also been armed with pieces that took obliquely everything heading for the town; in front of this formidable position all their light infantry had taken post with the field artillery'; '29th Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 9 November 1806'; 'meanwhile the enemy was fortifying himself at Lübeck'; 'the enemy had hastily arranged the old enceinte of Lübeck; he had placed batteries on the bastions; he did not doubt that he could gain a day there; but to see him, reconnoitre him and attack him was the affair of an instant'; 'from the Burgthor General Blücher rode to the Hörter-[Thor]'; '[Hörter-]Thor, where he handed the command to Colonel Görtzke, commander of the infantry regiment Owstien, showed him his position himself and gave him his instructions'; 'two horse guns were set up about 200 paces ahead with an escort, where a side road led left through the gardens, and secured against the onset of cavalry by felled trees'; 'the 4 battalion pieces were posted on the broken-down powder tower so that they could act on all sides and keep up a cross fire with the 6-pounder battery Lange on the high walls right and left of the Mühlenthor'; 'Marshal Soult to the Emperor. Lübeck, 6 November 1806'; 'General Legrand's division was charged with carrying the advanced work of the Mühlen gate'; 'a kind of hornwork, entirely detached and defended by 2 battalions, still held and put up a lively resistance; but it was also forced and all were taken'.

On p. 733, the sixth paragraph of Bernadotte's letter, on Colonel Gérard and General Maison, and the footnotes; the footnotes of p. 739 (the 1st corps's position on the evening of the 6th and two orders of 7 November), General L. Berthier's letter to General Dupont (pp. 739-740), the paragraphs of p. 740 between the passages transcribed, and the end of Bernadotte's letter with its postscript (p. 741); the Grand Duke of Berg's postscript, which continues on p. 746; the detailed list of the 1st corps's dead and wounded that Bernadotte's chief of staff was to send. Höpfner's pages between those transcribed (pp. 274-276, 278, 280-281, 285-286, 289-291, 296, 298), among them the defence of the Burgthor and Blücher's way through the town, and his plan of Lübeck. No figure seen only in the OCR is restated.

Most consequential gap: side A's strength and the forces engaged. Bodart's 30,000 is the only count read; the French letters name divisions and regiments without numbers, and Soult says not all his forces were needed. A return of the 1st and 4th corps and of the cavalry reserve for early November would bound it; the fold-out situation tables in Foucart's annexes (after p. 939), not read, are the nearest candidate, and the same follow-up would serve the Ratkau entry.

Disputes kept as separate claims: side B's strength (15,000, Bodart; about 20,000 on the rampart and around the town, with about 5,000 outside, the 1st corps journal; very few men at Lübeck, Bernadotte's letter of 4 in the morning; 13 battalions with later reinforcements and 52 guns, Höpfner); the prisoners of the day (about 4,000, Bodart and the 29th Bulletin; more than 5,000 with the Swedes, Bernadotte; at least 6,000, Soult; 5,000 men, the Grand Duke of Berg; 5—6000 lodged in the churches, Höpfner); the guns (more than 30, Bernadotte; at least 50, Soult and the Grand Duke; 60, the Bulletin; 22 without the regimental cannon, Höpfner; 25 for Legrand's division alone, the 4th corps); the Swedes (2,000 entered Lübeck, by Bernadotte's information; more than 600 taken, Bernadotte; 1,000 or 1,200, the Grand Duke; 1,600, the Bulletin); side A's loss (about 2,000, Bodart; more than 1,500 killed or wounded in the 1st corps, Bernadotte); the squadrons cut off after the town fell (4 with their guns, Soult; 4 that surrendered to the Grand Duke's cavalry, Bernadotte; 3 dragoon squadrons with 4 guns near Fackenburg, the 4th corps); and who directed side A's attack (the Grand Duke of Berg principally, Soult; the marshals' dispositions, the Grand Duke).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his sources for this entry were not checked; his about 4,000 prisoners equal the 29th Bulletin's 4,000); Foucart, t.
